lessons.title: The Breakeven Point: How Much You Must Claim for the Old Regime to Win

children.text: The seven-step method gives you an answer for one salary and one set of deductions. But what you really want to know is simpler: how much would I need to claim for the old regime to be worth it? That number is your breakeven. Once you know it, most regime decisions take ten seconds.

markDefs.definition: The total of old regime exemptions and deductions, over and above the ₹50,000 standard deduction, at which tax under both regimes is exactly equal.

children.text: is the amount of HRA, LTA, professional tax, 80C, 80CCD(1B), 80D, home loan interest and other old regime benefits you must claim, on top of the ₹50,000 standard deduction, so that old regime tax equals new regime tax. Claim more and the old regime wins. Claim less and the new regime wins.

body.caption: G is gross salary, D* is the breakeven deduction. Solve for D*. Employer NPS is ignored here, assuming it is the same amount in both regimes.

children.text: Worked example at ₹15 lakh salary. New regime taxable income is ₹14,25,000, and slab tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of ₹2,25,000, which is ₹93,750. Now find the old regime taxable income that also produces ₹93,750. Tax at ₹5 lakh is ₹12,500, so the remaining ₹81,250 must come from the 20% band: ₹81,250 ÷ 20% = ₹4,06,250 above ₹5 lakh, or ₹9,06,250 of taxable income. Breakeven deduction is ₹15,00,000 minus ₹50,000 minus ₹9,06,250, which is ₹5,43,750.

body.text: Look at the dip just above ₹12.75 lakh. Once you lose the new regime's rebate, the breakeven drops sharply to about ₹5.05 lakh near a ₹13.5 lakh salary. This is the salary band where the old regime is easiest to justify. Above that, the new regime's wider slabs keep pushing the bar higher until it settles at ₹8 lakh.

children.text: Above ₹24.75 lakh of salary, new regime taxable income is above ₹24 lakh and old regime taxable income is above ₹10 lakh. Every extra rupee is taxed at 30% in both, so the gap between them is fixed. Set the two tax formulas equal:

content.caption: The 0.3G terms cancel, leaving 0.3D* = ₹2,40,000, so D* = ₹8,00,000 at every salary in this zone (until surcharge applies above ₹50 lakh).

body.title: Find the Breakeven at ₹16 Lakh
body.prompt: Pranav, a chartered accountant working in-house at a Vadodara chemicals company, earns a gross salary of ₹16,00,000. What is his breakeven deduction beyond the ₹50,000 standard deduction?
body.explanation: New regime taxable income is ₹15,25,000, and slab tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of ₹3,25,000 (₹48,750), total ₹1,08,750. In the old regime, ₹1,08,750 minus ₹12,500 is ₹96,250, which at 20% needs ₹4,81,250 above ₹5 lakh, so taxable income of ₹9,81,250. Breakeven is ₹16,00,000 minus ₹50,000 minus ₹9,81,250, which is ₹5,68,750.

children.text: How Much Can You Realistically Claim?
Now put a ceiling on the other side. Take a salaried person under 60 who pays no rent, so no HRA, and who has maxed out every common deduction including a home loan.

body.caption: Maximum Common Deductions Without HRA (Under 60, Senior Citizen Parents)

body.text: ₹4.78 lakh is below the lowest breakeven of about ₹5.05 lakh. For a salaried taxpayer under 60 with no HRA, no LTA claim, no education loan and no large donations, the old regime cannot beat the new regime at any salary up to ₹50 lakh in tax year 2026-27.

This is why HRA decides so many outcomes. A metro renter can add ₹3 lakh to ₹6 lakh of HRA exemption on top of the list above, which is often the only way past ₹8 lakh. The other exceptions are large education loan interest under 80E, which has no cap, and big donations under 80G. LTA can tip the balance in a year you travel, especially near a ₹13.5 lakh salary where the bar is lowest, but it is capped at actual fares and only two journeys per four-year block.

body.title: Ten-Second Decision
body.question: Siddharth, a consultant in Delhi, earns ₹28 lakh. His old regime benefits beyond the standard deduction are HRA ₹4,20,000, 80C ₹1,50,000, 80CCD(1B) ₹50,000, 80D ₹25,000 and LTA ₹40,000, a total of ₹6,85,000. He has no employer NPS. Which regime is cheaper?
options: Old regime, because ₹6.85 lakh is a very large amount of deductions
New regime, because his total is below the ₹8 lakh breakeven for salaries above ₹24.75 lakh
Old regime, because HRA always makes the old regime better
body.explanation: At ₹28 lakh, the breakeven is ₹8 lakh. Siddharth claims ₹6,85,000, which is ₹1,15,000 short. The new regime wins by ₹1,15,000 × 30% × 1.04, which is ₹35,880.

body.title: Remember the Plateau
body.textWithBlank: For salaries above ₹24.75 lakh and up to ₹50 lakh, the old regime needs more than ₹___ lakh of benefits beyond the standard deduction to win.
body.explanation: In this zone both regimes tax the next rupee at 30%, so the breakeven stays fixed at ₹8 lakh.

body.title: Lakshmi Just Clears the Bar
body.scenario: Lakshmi, 38, is a vice president at a Mumbai asset management company earning ₹35 lakh, with a basic salary of ₹14 lakh. Her old regime benefits beyond the standard deduction are HRA ₹5,40,000, 80C ₹1,50,000, 80CCD(1B) ₹50,000, 80D ₹50,000 and professional tax ₹2,500, a total of ₹7,92,500. Her employer does not currently contribute to NPS.
body.prompt: Which regime wins today? Then suppose her employer offers employer NPS at the maximum each regime allows: 10% of basic in the old regime, 14% in the new. Does the answer change?
body.modelAnswer: Today, ₹7,92,500 is ₹7,500 short of the ₹8 lakh breakeven, so the new regime wins, by ₹7,500 × 30% × 1.04, which is ₹2,340. The two regimes are almost tied. If she adds just ₹7,500 more of genuine deductions, the old regime edges ahead. With employer NPS, the old regime gets ₹1,40,000 (10% of ₹14 lakh) and the new regime gets ₹1,96,000 (14%). The extra ₹56,000 in the new regime is worth ₹56,000 × 30% × 1.04, which is ₹17,472 more tax saved. The new regime would then win by ₹2,340 plus ₹17,472, which is ₹19,812. When the margin is this thin, small changes like a salary restructuring, a cheaper flat or a skipped NPS contribution flip the answer, so recheck every year.

body.text: These breakevens assume a resident under 60, salary as the only income, no special-rate capital gains, no surcharge and the same employer NPS in both regimes. Senior citizens have lower old regime slabs, so their breakevens are lower. If employer NPS is higher in the new regime, the bar for the old regime rises. When your situation differs, fall back on the full seven-step comparison.

body.title: Your Ten-Second Test
steps: Add up every old regime benefit beyond the ₹50,000 standard deduction: HRA, LTA, professional tax, 80C, 80CCD(1B), 80D, home loan interest, 80E, 80G, 80TTA
Find your salary's breakeven from the table, or use ₹8 lakh if your salary is above ₹24.75 lakh
If your salary is ₹12.75 lakh or less, pick the new regime, since the old regime can at best tie
If your total is well below breakeven, pick the new regime
If you are within about ₹50,000 of breakeven either way, run the full seven-step comparison before deciding

points: Breakeven is the amount of old regime benefits, beyond the ₹50,000 standard deduction, at which both regimes cost the same.
Up to ₹12.75 lakh of salary, the new regime is tax-free, so the old regime can only tie.
Between ₹12.75 lakh and ₹24.75 lakh, breakeven ranges from about ₹5.05 lakh to ₹8 lakh.
Above ₹24.75 lakh, breakeven is flat at ₹8 lakh because both regimes tax the next rupee at 30%.
Without HRA, the common maximum of about ₹4.78 lakh never reaches breakeven, so the new regime wins.
When you are close to breakeven, small changes like employer NPS or a rent change can flip the result.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Breakeven figures are illustrative calculations under the stated assumptions for tax year 2026-27, rounded to the nearest rupee, and do not cover every situation. Consult a qualified tax professional before filing.
